structure.title: A history of class conflict
structure.text: The opening presents capitalism as a transformative force and interprets society through antagonistic classes.

structure.title: Programme and rivals
structure.text: Later sections explain communist aims, answer objections, criticise competing socialisms, and identify political alliances.

people.name: Bourgeoisie
people.text: The class that owns factories, land and capital, which the manifesto credits with transforming the world and accuses of turning every relation into a cash transaction.

people.name: Proletariat
people.text: The working class, who own nothing but their labour, and who Marx and Engels argue will become the agents of the next revolution.

people.name: Class struggle
people.text: Their claim that the history of every society so far is the history of struggle between classes, from masters and slaves to capitalists and workers.

context.title: A manifesto
context.text: This is an intervention intended to mobilise, not a detached survey of every economic position. Description and exhortation continually reinforce each other.

context.title: Historical movement
context.text: The authors make large claims about capitalism's development and its opponents. Their confidence should not be confused with proof of inevitability.

notice.why: Capitalism's productive force helps generate the argument against it.

opening: Factories are transforming work, commerce reaches across the world, and arrangements that once seemed permanent are being swept away. Marx and Engels describe this upheaval with an admiration for capitalism's force that can surprise readers expecting only denunciation. Then they argue that the same system is producing the people who will overthrow it. This short declaration gives economic conflict the urgency of a historical showdown, making a case whose extraordinary political afterlife began with the claim that workers could recognise their common situation and act together.
